The ancestors said:
"We are the fathers, along with grandfathers / and great-grandfathers, of you who have not performed merit, suffering because of your wicked deed.
This is a hell, O fortunate one, in the form of a pit; / and you are the clump of vīraṇa grass, and we hang upon you."
"As long as you live, O brahmin, for that long only do we stay [here]. / When you die, we, sinners in mind, shall go to hell.13

If you take a wife and produce an offspring / endowed with superior virtues, we might be freed from this, one by one.14
Not by any other austerity, my son, nor by the fruit of sacred fords [can we be freed]. / Therefore do this, O wise one; deliver your ancestors from fear."15
Having agreed with "So be it," and having worshipped the Bull-bannered [Śiva], / he raised his ancestors from the pit and made them leaders of the gaṇas.16
And he himself, dear to Rudra, named Sukeśa by name, / honoured and mighty, became a leader of Rudra's gaṇas.17
"Therefore, performing fierce austerity, produce an offspring / exceptionally endowed with virtues, O king of mountains; then you will obtain renown."18
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the seer, the king of mountains, steadfast in his vow, / performed vast austerity by which Brahmā was pleased.19
Then Brahmā came to him and spoke, saying, "I am the granter of boons. / Speak; I am pleased with you, O mountain, by this austerity, O one of noble vows."20

Himavat said:
"O Lord, I desire a son adorned with all virtues. / Grant this boon if you are pleased with us, O Lord."21
Brahmā said:
"A maiden shall be your daughter, O king of mountains, a fair-complexioned one, / through whose power you will obtain abundant renown everywhere;22 / worshipped by all the gods, surrounded by crores of sacred fords, / purifying and holy, everywhere even for the gods.
And she shall be your eldest [daughter], and after her two other auspicious ones."23
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, Brahmā vanished right there. / And in course of time, that king of mountains begot upon Menā24

Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and also Ekapāṭalā. / Ekaparṇā took recourse to a banyan tree, and Ekapāṭalā to a trumpet-flower tree.25
The two took shelter [there], but Aparṇā, homeless, performed austerity / difficult to be performed by gods and demons, for a hundred thousand years.26
That Ekaparṇā lived on a diet of a single leaf; / and Ekapāṭalā sustained herself on a single trumpet-flower.27
Every full thousand [years], the two took food; / but Aparṇā was without food. Her mother spoke to her,28
Forbidding her, saying: "O mā" (Oh, do not!), afflicted by motherly affection. / Addressed thus by her mother at that time, the goddess, practising severe [austerities], / became celebrated in the worlds and worshipped by the gods by that very name [Umā].29

This world of moving and unmoving beings is guarded by the three maidens. / By the austerity of these [maidens], as long as the earth endures, [she] will sustain the worlds.30
All three had bodies made of austerity, endowed with the power of yoga; / and all were great yoginīs, all of constant youth.31
They are the mothers of the worlds and celibates as well; / and they constantly bless the worlds with their own austerity.32

Among them, Umā is the most excellent and the eldest, fair-complexioned, / possessed of the power of great yoga, who attended upon Mahādeva. / And Uśanas, that son of Bhṛgu, became her adopted son. / Ekaparṇā, however, gave birth to a son, Devala, [begotten] by Asita.33-34
The third of those maidens, Ekapāṭalā, / approached Jaigīṣavya, the son of Śataśalāka.35
His sons Śaṅkha and Likhita are known to have not been born of a womb. / But that fair-complexioned Umā whom I mentioned to you—36
Then, perceiving the entire triple world scorched / by the power of her austerity, Brahmā spoke [these] words:37 / Brahmā said:
"O goddess, why will you scorch the worlds with your austerity, O fair one? / This universe was created by you; having made it, do not destroy it.38

said to him after honoring the brahmin with water for the feet, argha offering, and madhuparka—she of beautiful eyes, dear to brahmins:

“O lord, I am not independent; my father and mother are [my authorities].
They are the masters regarding my giving away; I am a maiden, O best of the twice-born.
Go and ask my father, the imperishable king of mountains.
If he gives me to you, O vipra, that is pleasing to me.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed god, the lord, deformed just in that way,
said to that king of mountains: “O protector of the mountain, give me Umā.”

and possessing all fragrances, you shall be exceedingly dear to the goddess.
Without fear among all worlds you shall wander, well contented.
And this hermitage, famed as Citrakūṭa,
whoever approaches seeking merit, shall obtain [the fruit of] an Aśvamedha;
and dying anywhere [here], he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
And whoever, observing restrictions here, properly casts off his life-breaths,
endowed with the tapas of the goddess, shall become a great leader of the Gaṇas.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the god, the creator of the universe, the lord and master of all beings,
took leave of the daughter of the Himavat and vanished.

On the vast back of the Himālaya, crowded with hundreds of aerial chariots, / the svayaṃvara of the Mountain's daughter took place in course of time.
Then Himavān, king of mountains, skilled in meditation, / having learned through that counsel that his daughter was sought by the God of gods,
though knowing [this], the great mountain, desiring to follow traditional custom, / proclaimed the svayaṃvara of the goddess throughout all the worlds:
“So that before gods, dānavas, and siddhas who inhabit all worlds, / my daughter may choose the Supreme Lord,
that will be a praiseworthy good deed, approved for my prosperity.” / Thinking thus, the lord of mountains, holding Maheśvara in his heart,
making the place strewn with jewels, for the goddess, / throughout worlds reaching up to Brahmā, that best of mountain lords held the svayaṃvara.

Then, as soon as the svayaṃvara of the Mountain's daughter was thus proclaimed, O Vyāsa, / the gods and other inhabitants of the whole universe arrived, clad in divine attire. / Seated upon an expanded lotus seat, surrounded by siddhas and immeasurable yogins,
solicited by that king of mountains, the Grandfather [Brahmā] arrived there.
Bearing a thousand eyes, the king of gods, noble in appearance with divine gestures and garlands, / [mounted] Airāvata, foremost among all lordly elephants, who created a flowing stream of rut-juice;
having mounted him, bearing his thunderbolt, that king of all immortals arrived before the gods. / Vivasvān, divine in form, supreme in fiery brilliance and majesty, illuminating all directions,
having mounted a golden aerial chariot with fluttering banners, arrived swiftly with great speed. / Wearing brilliant ear-rings blazing with gems, upon an aerial chariot resembling the brilliance of fire and sun,
the son of the sage Kaśyapa, the āditya bearing the name Bhaga, approached near, / his staff-like limbs plump, his movements graceful, endowed with power equal to his brilliance, strength, and command.

While the goddess stood holding the garland in the assembly of the gods, / when the gods headed by Śakra had arrived, having gathered for the svayaṃvara,

Then she, of pure resolve, having attained the noble fruit she had desired, / remained as if contented, having held him alone in her heart.
Then, seeing the child resting in the goddess's lap, / the gods conferred, saying, "Who is this here?" and became exceedingly afflicted and enraged.
The slayer of Vṛtra raised his arm and summoned his thunderbolt against him; / that arm of his remained lifted up, frozen just like that.
Paralyzed by Śambhu, the god of gods in the form of a child, / he was unable to throw the thunderbolt, nor could he move his arm.
Then the powerful god, the Āditya born of Kaśyapa named Bhaga, / bewildered, raised a blazing club and wished to throw it.
The Lord paralyzed his arm too in the very same way at that moment. / Shaking his head, Viṣṇu angrily glared at him.
The god indeed caused the hair of his head to fall out. / Grinding his teeth with his teeth, Pūṣan glared at Śarva, bewildered.

"You are the unborn, the immortal God, the creator, the destroyer, the supreme, all-pervading Lord, / the primordial matter, the spirit, reality, the Absolute that is to be meditated upon, the imperishable;
the immortal, the Supreme Self, Īśvara, the great cause, / the author of the Vedas, the creator of nature, the creator of all, the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, O Lord of the gods of gods, you cannot be known by the celestials, / nor, O God, can you be known even by the sages who know yoga.
Incomprehensible, O Great God, you exist by your own sport; / in the great creation and the great cosmic cycle, you alone abide, O Lord.
Even I do not know your action, O Maheśvara; / how can the gods comprehend that which is profound and unfathomable in essence?
And this Prakṛti, O God, is always the cause of your creation; / assuming the form of a wife, she has arrived as the cause of the universe.
Salutations to you always, O Īśāna, and salutations always to the Goddess! / By your grace and command, O Lord of the gods, these creatures—
the gods and others—were created by me, [yet] they are foolish and deluded by your mystic power. / Bestow your grace upon them, so that they may become as they were before."

7.2.m:
When that season had approached the mountain to attend the marriage of the Mountain's Daughter, / clumps of trees and shrubs, wearing floral crests, appeared on every side.
Fragrant, delightful, and very cool breezes blew repeatedly, / their forms full of masses of pollen from the tips of diverse flowers, stirring the passion of gods and celestial women. / And likewise, lotus ponds filled with clear water and adorned with blossoms of water lilies and lotuses / became exceedingly charming, like women whose breast-tips have slightly blossomed forth.
By the nature of the season and by the rising of intoxication, / male cuckoos, their wings folded among the blossoming branches, / sang clearly, delighting the ears of the celestial maidens.
The chief celestial elephants, rejoicing, drank the lake waters, / neither too hot nor too cold, colored tawny by powdered filaments, / and made to resound by pairs of cakravāka birds. / […] covered with priyaṅgu blossoms […]
shone with their blossoms, as if mutually reproaching one another.

Blossoming aśoka creepers clinging to the sāl trees shone there / like loving women with their bodies clinging to the necks of their beloveds. / Clustered with blossoms on creepers sung over by swarms of impassioned bees, / the jasmine vines shone, as though conversing with one another.

On wide expanses of water, lotus clusters arose on all sides: / golden in some, emerald-colored throughout in others, / and with stems of cat's-eye gems in yet other lakes.
Charming ponds were there, adorned with lotuses and water lilies, / echoing with diverse birds, and fitted with flights of golden steps.
The lofty, closely packed peaks of that mountain, / covered with fully blossomed karṇikāras, shone as if made of gold, O sage.
All the directions became pale red with pāṭala flowers slightly blossoming, / their forms swaying in the breeze. / Blue aśoka trees, resembling the peaks of the black collyrium mountain, / flourished in full bloom upon the mountain, as if competing with one another.
And groves of kiṃśuka trees, humming with large black bees, / sprang up everywhere upon the slopes of the mountain.

7.2.m:
The beauty of that Himavat then came from thickets of tamāla trees, / as if masses of dark clouds had nestled into its ravines. / With trees full of blossoms, bearing very wide branches and rising high, / and with the chatter of intoxicated male cuckoos, the Snowy Mountain shone exceedingly then.
Hearing the sounds of the cuckoos on all sides, melodious with the intoxication of the season,
peacocks with fluttering feathers cried out sweet notes. / His power enhanced by their calls, bow and arrow of flowers in hand,
the bodiless Ananga made ready to pierce the celestial women in their limbs.
Summer too, with its fierce sun and mostly warm waters, / came to the Snowy Mountain to attend the wedding of the goddess.

Likewise, kurabaka trees also, their forms pale white with blossoms, / flourished on all the peaks, frequented by swarms of bees.
And bakula trees on the broad ridges of the mountain / released charming flowers all around.
Thus, clothed entirely in varied flowers, their regions lovely with the diverse calls of birds, / the six seasons arrived, O best of sages, for the prosperity of the wedding of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain.
Then, as this gathering of all beings was proceeding, / filled with various musical instruments, Brahmā, my father, himself,
having adorned the daughter of the mountain with a wealth of suitable ornaments, / brought her into the city, he who knows the world, taking [...].
Then Brahmā again addressed the Lord, the all-pervading one: / 'Stationed in the role of preceptor, I offer oblation into the fire.
If you give me the command, this ritual procedure must be performed.' / Śaṅkara, the god, the god of gods, the lord of the world, said to that god:

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, entitled 'The Marriage of Umā', in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, when the wedding of Bhava of boundless splendor was complete, / experiencing supreme joy, the gods along with the Grandfather / praised Maheśvara with pleasing words, bowing down: / 'Homage to the mountain-liṅga, homage indeed to the Lord of the mountain!
Homage to the one swift as the wind, to the misshapen one, and to the unconquered one! / Homage to the destroyer of affliction and the giver of auspicious prosperity!' / [Apparatus readings: 163 vai devadevasya - gha; 164 śca - ka; 165 kṛtvā - ka; 166 mupa... - ka; 167 ... ta - ka; 168 haviḥ - gha; 169 triṣu - gha; 170 stutvā - gha; 171 hasita - gha; 172 sarvadaivataiḥ - gha; 173 siddhaiḥ - gha; 174 ... le - ka, gha.]

Homage to the one with blue locks, homage to the husband of Ambikā! / Homage to the one whose form is the wind, homage indeed to the one of a hundred forms! / Homage to the one of fearsome form, and to the one of misformed eyes! / Homage to the thousand-eyed one and to the thousand-footed one!
Homage to the mystery of the Vedas, homage, homage to the limbs of the Veda! / To the paralyzer of Śakra's arm, to the sprout of the Veda's limbs! / Homage, homage to the master of the moving and unmoving, to the restrainer! / To the liṅga reposing upon the waters, to the one who possesses an expansive liṅga at the end of the cosmic age!
Homage to the one with a garland of skulls, homage to the one crowned with skulls! / Homage to the one with a skull in hand, to the fanged one, homage to the mace-bearer!
Homage to the lord of the three worlds, and to the one bowed to by the seven worlds! / Homage to the one with a club in hand, and to the dispeller of distress of the Pramathas!
Homage to the destroyer of the head of the sacrifice, to the remover of Kṛṣṇa's hair! / To the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes, and to the extractor of Pūṣan's teeth!
Homage to the wielder of the Pināka, the trident, the sword, the scimitar, and the mallet! / Homage be to the death of Death, and to the three-eyed one!

Sanatkumāra said:
O son of Parāśara, he who hears or recites this hymn of praise, / going to the heavenly world, is honored like the king of immortals. (30)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, named 'The Hymn on the Marriage of Umā', in the Skandapurāṇa.

His wife, exceedingly grief-stricken, wailed piteously; / weeping, she, inspiring pity, begged the god and the goddess. (8) / Hearing her crying, those two compassionate deities / looked upon her, comforted that sorrowful woman, and said: (9)
"He has certainly been burned, O auspicious one, and his rebirth here is not intended. / Even without a body, he will perform all your purposes in due time. (10)
When Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva, O beautiful one, / then this one will indeed become his son, and will be your husband, O Rati!" (11)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having obtained that boon, Kāma's wife of auspicious countenance / went to her desired place, filled with delight, her distress dispelled. (12)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus burned foolish-minded Kāma, Śaṅkara / addressed the daughter of the Himavat on account of the devotion of that best of sages. (13)

7.2.m:
"You have asked me, O Śakti, and he shall be born to you: / one equal to you, knowing all the Vedas, belonging to you, O bull among sages.
And just as the self of the seed, born indeed by itself through the inner self, / does not remain in the form of seed once it undergoes another transformation,
even so that self of our self, born and designated as offspring, / will not remain in his original self, having undergone another transformation."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to him, laughing as he looked on, / the yogi of supreme splendor suddenly vanished from sight.
When that Mahādeva had gone, your grandfather Śakti, / reflecting upon those words, thought, 'So indeed it shall be.'
Then, after a great deal of time, bestowing auspiciousness, had passed, / consecrated through great austerity, possessing the radiance of fire,
he placed an excellent embryo in Adṛśyantī, O one of great wisdom. / While she was carrying that child, King Kalmāṣapāda, enraged, / his senses hijacked by a rakṣasa, devoured the seer.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.2.m:
the gods together with the sages said to that son of Gādhi:
"Vasiṣṭha is possessed of great fiery energy, and you, son of Gādhi, are righteous.
Both of you are immortal, free from old age, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga.
Indeed, there is no destruction for either of you, nor will you destroy [one another].
Yet while both of you fight each other, [destruction comes] upon the gods and all the worlds,
just as when two rutting elephants fight in the forest,
a great destruction of creepers and trees occurs due to their trampling;
even so, by the enmity arisen between you two great-souled ones,
misfortune will clearly befall the worlds, of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, destruction […] of the worlds along with the seers.
Let there be friendship between you two, and an end to enmity."
Being addressed thus by the sages together with the gods, the son of Gādhi,
astonished then by [Vasiṣṭha's] fiery splendor, said to them, "So be it!"
Then all the celestials addressed Vasiṣṭha in the same way.

7.2.m:
Any brahmin who listens to this, or recites it to brahmins,
crosses over insurmountable perils, his prowess unflagging.
He shall be elevated through nobility, pleasant pastimes, and the goodness of three generations of ancestors, radiant and beautifully adorned;
he shall become equal to the king of all the gods and shall disport at will in heaven.
Thus it transpired, O Vyāsa, between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha:
their enmity was brought to an end, for the welfare of the worlds once again.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, named 'The Cessation of Enmity', in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.2.m:
And he, not born from a womb, having propitiated Maheśvara,
attained equality with Rudra and shone forth as the Great Lord of the Gaṇas.
Vyāsa said:
How was Nandin born, and how, having propitiated Śaṃkara,
did he attain equality with Śambhu and the status of [His] door-keeper?
Sanatkumāra said:
That twice-born saw his ancestors hanging down, devoid of refuge,
fallen into a dreadful hell because of the severing of their lineage.
Desiring an offspring, he was told by them: "Propitiate that imperishable god of the world,
propitiate Mahādeva for the sake of a son, O best of the twice-born!
He who is capable of delivering [us] will grant you a son."
Hearing their words, he then went for refuge to Śiva.
As he practiced austerities for a thousand years, the trident-bearer,
Śarva, accompanied by Umā and surrounded by the gaṇas, spoke to him: "I am the granter of boons!"

“O Sālaṅkāyana, this is that son given to you formerly by the god Śambhu, / not born of a womb; greet him with joy! (33)
Because he causes joy to you at all times, O best of the twice-born, / therefore this son of yours shall be called by the name of Nandī.” (34)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, at the word of the wind, he embraced Nandī; / taking him, he brought him who delighted the eyes to his hermitage. (35)
He performed the rites for him, beginning with the tonsure, naming, and vows. / Having done so, he instructed him fully in the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences, (36)

named Mitra and Varuṇa, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, / knowing all beings in the three worlds, moving and unmoving— (45)
encouraged by them, he too sat down on an excellent seat. / […] (46)

“For what reason did both of you, O best of sages, / not bestow upon my fortunate son the blessing of long life?” (50)
Mitra and Varuṇa said:
“This son of yours, dear friend, is recognized by all as short-lived; / he will retain his life for only one more year from now.” (51)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, tormented by grief, distressed by calamity concerning his child, / having dismissed the two tiger-like seers, he lamented alone. (52)
Hearing his clear voice as he lamented in grief, his son / Nandī came to him and saw his father extremely grieved. (53)
Nandī said:
“By what sorrow are you tormented and weeping, father? / From where has your distress arisen? I wish to know, father.” (54)

Sanatkumāra said:
Knowing him to speak thus, uttering words with a pure mind, / the [father of] great austerity, unbroken in spirit, sent forth his son with fortitude.
Having saluted his father's feet with his head, he of great renown, / having made a circumambulation, departed with resolve.

Having saluted all the seers, that sage of noble intellect, wishing to see [him], / with his mind fixed on the god, [set out towards] Śiva who removes the distress of the bowed. / Thus in the Skandapurāṇa ends the twentieth chapter, named "Nandin's Entry into Austerity".

Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone forth then, Nandin went to the best of rivers, / known as Bhuvanā, which brings welfare to all worlds.
Entering it, the wise, radiant one stood one-pointed. / Afraid of death, collected in mind, he then murmured prayers to Rudra.
As he was murmuring prayers right there, intent on that, desiring that blessing, / when one ten-million had been recited, then the god was pleased.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having immersed himself again, self-restrained in the very same way, / he murmured another ten-million [recitations], contemplating only Rudra.

Then, when the second ten-million was completed, the bull-bannered [god] / approached him and said: "I am a granter of boons!"
He said: "O Blessed One, Lord of Gods, I wish to recite / an additional third ten-million by your grace, O omnipresent one!"

The God of Gods said:
"O son of Śilāda, I am a granter of boons to you, pleased by this austerity. / Well has it been recited by you, wise one! Tell what is in your heart."
The son of Śilāda said:
"May I recite yet another ten-million through your fiery power! / I choose this boon, O God, if you are pleased with me, O omnipresent one!"
The Blessed One said:
"O son of Śilāda, [...] I, together with Ambikā, am pleased with you. / Whatever desire you choose today, all that I grant to you.
The state of Brahmā, or the state of Viṣṇu, or the state of Indra, or any other state— / become the sun or Rudra! Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
Sanatkumāra said:
He, thus addressed by the god, bowed his head at [his] feet / and praised the destroyer of the cities, of the body of Kāma, of the sacrifice, and of the mountain:
